title: World Energy Use
lead: The world runs on energy, and most of it still comes from sources that can be used up. This section sets out where the world’s energy comes from and how the mix has changed, how fast the demand for it is growing, how closely a country’s economic well-being follows its energy use, and why energy resources have to be conserved even though the law of conservation of energy says that no energy is ever lost.
objectives: Describe the distinction between renewable and nonrenewable energy sources.
Explain why the inevitable conversion of energy to less useful forms makes it necessary to conserve energy resources.
summary_html:
• The relative use of different fuels to provide energy has changed over the years, but fuel use is currently dominated by oil, although natural gas and solar contributions are increasing.
  • Although non-renewable sources dominate, some countries meet a sizeable percentage of their electricity needs from renewable resources.
  • The United States obtains only about 10% of its energy from renewable sources, mostly hydroelectric power.
  • Economic well-being is dependent upon energy use, and in most countries higher standards of living, as measured by GDP (Gross Domestic Product) per capita, are matched by higher levels of energy consumption per capita.
  • Even though, in accordance with the law of conservation of energy, energy can never be created or destroyed, energy that can be used to do work is always partly converted to less useful forms, such as waste heat to the environment, in all of our uses of energy for practical purposes.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between energy conservation and the law of conservation of energy? Give some examples of each.

answer.solution: The law of the conservation of energy is a statement about nature: the total amount of energy in an isolated system always remains constant, and no exception to it has ever been found. It holds whether or not anyone attends to it, and it is what lets you say that the chemical energy in a tank of petrol is all still accounted for after the car has driven and stopped, some of it in the motion the car had, the rest in the warmed brakes, the warmed air and the exhaust. Energy conservation is a different thing: it is the philosophy of seeking to decrease the amount of energy an individual or a group uses. It is done in two ways, by reducing activities, such as turning down a thermostat or driving fewer kilometers, and by increasing conversion efficiencies, as a more efficient room heater, a car with a greater miles-per-gallon rating and an energy-efficient compact fluorescent light all do. The first is a bookkeeping rule about a quantity; the second is a choice about a resource, and it is worth making because the end of most energy transformations is waste heat that can no longer do work.

exercises.prompt: If the efficiency of a coal-fired electrical generating plant is 35%, then what do we mean when we say that energy is a conserved quantity?

answer.solution: All of the energy released in burning the coal is still there after the plant has run. About 35% of it leaves the plant as electrical energy, and the other 65% leaves as heat transferred to the cooling water, to the air and to the surroundings through the exhaust. None of it has been created and none of it has been destroyed, so the total before and the total after are the same, and that is what it means to call energy a conserved quantity. The efficiency measures something else: how much of that energy is still in a form useful for doing work. The 65% has been degraded to waste heat in the environment, and although it is still energy, it can no longer turn a generator, which is why the coal is a resource that can be used up even though the energy in it is not.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the force the woman in the figure exerts to do a push-up at constant speed, taking all data to be known to three digits. (b) How much work does she do if her center of mass rises 0.240 m? (c) What is her useful power output if she does 25 push-ups in 1 min? (Should work done lowering her body be included? See the discussion of useful work in Work, Energy, and Power in Humans.)

parts.hint: Her weight acts downward at her center of gravity, 0.900 m from her feet, and the force from the floor acts upward on her arms, 1.50 m from her feet. Balance the two about her feet.
The force on her arms is in the direction her center of mass rises, so the work is that force times the 0.240 m.
Useful power output is the useful work done divided by the time it took. Only the work of raising her body counts, so take 25 times the work of part (b) over 1 min.

exercises.prompt: The 70.0-kg swimmer in Work, Energy, and Power in Humans starts a race with an initial velocity of 1.25 m/s and exerts an average force of 80.0 N backward with his arms during each 1.80 m long stroke. (a) What is his initial acceleration if water resistance is 45.0 N? (b) What is the subsequent average resistance force from the water during the 5.00 s it takes him to reach his top velocity of 2.50 m/s? (c) Discuss whether water resistance seems to increase linearly with velocity.

parts.hint: The net external force on him is the 80.0 N forward from his arms less the 45.0 N of water resistance, and Newton’s second law turns that into an acceleration.
Over the 5.00 s his velocity rises from 1.25 m/s to 2.50 m/s, so find the average acceleration first and then the resistance that leaves that much net force.

answer.solution: (a) $0.500\ \text{m/s}^{2}$ (b) $62.5\ \text{N}$ (c) Assuming the acceleration of the swimmer decreases linearly with time over the 5.00 s interval, the frictional force must therefore be increasing linearly with time, since $f = F - ma$. If the acceleration decreases linearly with time, the velocity will contain a term dependent on time squared ($t^{2}$). Therefore, the water resistance will not depend linearly on the velocity.

exercises.prompt: (a) What force must be supplied by an elevator cable to produce an acceleration of $0.800\ \text{m/s}^{2}$ against a 200-N frictional force, if the mass of the loaded elevator is 1500 kg? (b) How much work is done by the cable in lifting the elevator 20.0 m? (c) What is the final speed of the elevator if it starts from rest? (d) How much work went into thermal energy?

parts.hint: Three forces act along the cable: the weight of the loaded elevator, the 200 N of friction and the pull of the cable. Newton’s second law gives the pull that leaves the stated acceleration.
The cable pulls in the direction the elevator moves, so the work it does is its force times the 20.0 m.
Take the net work, which is the work of the cable less the work against the weight and against friction, and set it equal to the change in kinetic energy from rest.
Friction is the only nonconservative force here, so the energy that went to thermal energy is the frictional force times the distance travelled.

exercises.prompt: Body fat is metabolized, supplying 9.30 kcal/g, when dietary intake is less than needed to fuel metabolism. The manufacturers of an exercise bicycle claim that you can metabolize 0.500 kg of fat per day by vigorously exercising for 2.00 h per day on their machine. (a) How many kcal are supplied by the metabolization of 0.500 kg of fat? (b) Calculate the kcal/min that you would have to utilize to metabolize fat at the rate of 0.500 kg in 2.00 h. (c) What is unreasonable about the results? (d) Which premise is unreasonable, or which premises are inconsistent?

parts.hint: Half a kilogram is 500 g, and each gram supplies 9.30 kcal.
Spread the energy of part (a) over the 2.00 h, written in minutes.

answer.solution: (a) $4.65 \times 10^{3}\ \text{kcal}$ (b) $38.8\ \text{kcal/min}$ (c) This power output is higher than the highest value on Table 7.5, which is about 35 kcal/min (corresponding to 2415 watts) for sprinting. (d) It would be impossible to maintain this power output for 2 hours (imagine sprinting for 2 hours!).

exercises.prompt: A 105-kg basketball player crouches down 0.400 m while waiting to jump. After exerting a force on the floor through this 0.400 m, their feet leave the floor and their center of gravity rises 0.950 m above its normal standing erect position. (a) Using energy considerations, calculate the player's velocity when they leave the floor. (b) What average force did the player exert on the floor? (Do not neglect the force to support their weight as well as that to accelerate them.) (c) What was the player's power output during the acceleration phase?

parts.hint: All of the kinetic energy the player has on leaving the floor becomes gravitational potential energy at the top of the rise of 0.950 m.
The work the player does through the 0.400 m has to supply both the kinetic energy of part (a) and the energy of raising the body through that 0.400 m.
Power is the work done divided by the time it took, and the time of the acceleration phase follows from the 0.400 m covered while the speed rose from zero to the answer of part (a).
